blocks.text:
A single deployable application is the simplest unit to build, test, deploy and reason about. It stops being adequate when the number of developers working on it prevents independent release, when parts of the system need very different scaling or availability characteristics, or when one failure domain takes down unrelated functionality. A microservice architecture addresses these organisational and scaling constraints by decomposing a system into independently deployable services, each owning a narrow business capability and its own data.

The decomposition is not free. Every in-process method call that becomes a network call acquires latency, a failure mode, a serialisation cost and a versioning problem. Every transaction that crossed a table boundary becomes a distributed consistency problem. The remainder of this Part is largely a catalogue of the mechanisms that make those costs manageable: timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, sagas, outbox tables, tracing and contract design. This first chapter establishes the vocabulary and the criteria that decide whether the cost is justified at all.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Three architectural styles

Three styles occupy the practical design space. A **monolith** is one deployable unit with one process and, usually, one database. A **modular monolith** is also one deployable unit, but its internal structure enforces module boundaries: each module owns its tables, exposes a small public API, and is forbidden from reaching into the internals of another. **Microservices** place each module in its own deployable unit with its own database, and the boundaries become network boundaries.

blocks.text:
The modular monolith is frequently the correct intermediate step. Its boundaries are cheap to move because a refactoring is a code change rather than a data migration between databases. Spring Modulith (a separate project built on Spring Boot 3) provides verification of module dependencies and application events between modules; the same rules can be enforced with ArchUnit tests. A service extracted later from a well-formed module inherits an already minimal interface.

#### Bounded contexts

The unit of decomposition in a sound design is the **bounded context** from domain-driven design: a region of the domain within which each term has exactly one meaning and one model. The word "product" illustrates the point. In a catalogue context a product has a description, images and categories. In an inventory context it is a stock keeping unit with a warehouse quantity. In a billing context it is a tax category and a unit price at a point in time. Forcing one shared `Product` class across all three produces a model that every team must change for every other team's reason. Separate contexts hold separate models and exchange only the data that the other side needs, typically by identifier.

blocks.title: Definition
blocks.text: Bounded context. A boundary within which a domain model and its vocabulary are consistent. Two contexts may use the same word for different concepts; translation between them occurs at an explicit interface (an anti-corruption layer, a published event schema or an API contract).

A **context map** records the relationships: which context is upstream (publishes a model), which is downstream (consumes it), and whether the consumer adapts to the producer (conformist), insulates itself with a translation layer (anti-corruption layer), or participates in a shared kernel. In service terms an anti-corruption layer is the mapper class that converts the remote DTO of another service into the local domain object, so that a change in the remote schema affects one class.

#### Database per service

Each service owns its persistent state and no other service reads or writes it directly. Access occurs only through the owning service's API or its published events. This rule is the one that distinguishes microservices from a monolith that merely happens to run in several processes. The consequences are structural:

- A join across two services is impossible in SQL. The caller composes the result in code (API composition), maintains a local read model fed by events (CQRS), or the data is duplicated deliberately.
- A transaction spanning two services cannot be an ACID transaction. Consistency is achieved through sagas and idempotent messages (see the chapter on distributed data).
- Each service may select a storage technology suited to its workload (relational for orders, a document store for the catalogue, a key-value store for sessions), at the cost of operating several technologies.
- A schema change is local to the owner, which removes the largest source of cross-team coordination.

#### Granularity, ownership and Conway's law

Conway's law states that the structure of a system mirrors the communication structure of the organisation that builds it. The practical corollary is the **inverse Conway manoeuvre**: the team structure is arranged first to match the desired architecture. A service owned by three teams has three sets of priorities and is released at the speed of the slowest negotiation; a service owned by one team that is also responsible for it in production (build it, run it) has a single decision maker.

Granularity has no universal measure. The following heuristics are useful in order of reliability:

1. **Data ownership.** A service should own a coherent set of entities and the invariants between them. If two candidate services must always be updated atomically, they are one service.
2. **Rate of change.** Code that changes together belongs together. If every feature requires coordinated changes in three services, the boundaries are wrong.
3. **Team ownership.** One team can reasonably own and operate a few services. A service that requires more than one team indicates a boundary that is too coarse.
4. **Scaling and failure profile.** A component with a distinct load profile (image resizing, search) or a distinct availability requirement (payment capture) is a candidate for isolation.
5. **Size is not a criterion.** Lines of code and the number of endpoints do not determine correct granularity. A service that can be rewritten by a small team in a few weeks is a useful sanity check, not a rule.

#### The costs, quantified

Two calculations explain most of the operational cost of fine-grained decomposition. First, availability multiplies. If a request requires five services in series and each is available 99.9 percent of the time, the request succeeds with probability 0.999 raised to the fifth power, about 99.5 percent. Second, tail latency amplifies with fan-out: if each call exceeds its own 99th percentile latency one time in a hundred, a request that makes 100 such calls sees at least one slow call 63 percent of the time. The program in the Hands-on section computes both.

blocks.text:
The eight fallacies of distributed computing (the network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite, the network is secure, topology does not change, there is one administrator, transport cost is zero, the network is homogeneous) are each violated by the first remote call that replaces a method call. A service developer must handle each of them explicitly in code and configuration.

#### When not to use microservices

The following conditions favour a monolith or a modular monolith, and a decomposition attempted without them tends to produce a distributed monolith (services that must be deployed together and fail together):

- The domain is not yet understood. Boundaries drawn early are usually wrong, and moving a boundary between services costs far more than moving it between packages.
- The organisation has few teams. Independent deployment is valuable only when more than one team wants to deploy independently.
- There is no automated delivery pipeline, no centralised logging, no metrics and no distributed tracing. Without these, a failure spanning four services cannot be diagnosed.
- The workload needs strong consistency across the entities that would be split, for example a ledger.
- The team lacks the capacity to operate additional infrastructure (a registry or Kubernetes, a gateway, a broker, per-service databases).

blocks.text:
#### Decomposition techniques

Two approaches dominate. **Decomposition by business capability** identifies what the business does (catalogue management, order fulfilment, payment) and creates one service per capability. **Decomposition by subdomain** uses the domain-driven design classification into core, supporting and generic subdomains; core subdomains receive the most investment and the most careful boundaries, generic ones (identity, notifications) are candidates for off-the-shelf products.

For an existing monolith the standard migration technique is the **strangler fig** pattern: a routing layer (the API gateway) is placed in front of the monolith, one capability at a time is reimplemented as a service, and the gateway route for that capability is switched from the monolith to the new service. The monolith shrinks until it can be retired or remains as a small core. Because the route can be switched back, each step is reversible.

### Worked example

The worked example used through this Part is an e-commerce platform decomposed along business capabilities. Seven services and one gateway result:

blocks.text:
The design applies four rules that recur in later chapters. Services call each other synchronously only when the caller cannot answer its own request without the answer (the order service needs a price and a stock check before accepting an order). State changes that other services merely react to (order placed, payment captured, shipment dispatched) are published as events. The order service owns the checkout process and its compensations. The gateway is the only component reachable from outside the cluster.

#### Repository and build layout

A multi-module Maven layout with a parent that imports the Spring Boot and Spring Cloud bills of materials keeps dependency versions consistent without coupling the services at run time. Each service remains an independently built and released artifact; the parent only fixes versions.

**Repository layout**

blocks.code:
shop-platform/
├── pom.xml                      parent: Boot parent, Spring Cloud BOM, shared plugin versions
├── api-gateway/                 Spring Cloud Gateway application
├── catalog-service/
├── inventory-service/
├── order-service/
│   ├── pom.xml
│   └── src/main/java/com/shop/order/
│       ├── OrderServiceApplication.java
│       ├── api/                 controllers, request and response DTOs
│       ├── domain/              entities, domain events, repository interfaces
│       ├── application/         use cases (services), transaction boundaries
│       └── infrastructure/      HTTP clients to other services, outbox, configuration
├── payment-service/
├── shipping-service/
├── customer-service/
└── notification-service/

blocks.text: The package layout inside a service follows the same discipline as the module layout in a modular monolith: `api` depends on `application`, `application` on `domain`, and only `infrastructure` knows about remote services. The class that calls the inventory service lives in `infrastructure`, and it returns a local type, which keeps the remote schema out of the domain.

blocks.text:
Spring Cloud release trains are matched to Spring Boot lines: the 2024.0.x train targets Boot 3.4, the 2025.0.x train targets Boot 3.5, and 2025.1.x targets Boot 4.0. Using a train with a Boot version outside its range produces startup failures of the kind `NoSuchMethodError` or a failed compatibility check, so the pair is always taken from the Spring Cloud project page. At the time of writing the Boot 3.4 and 3.5 lines are past open-source support and Boot 4.0 with Spring Cloud 2025.1.x is current; the mechanisms in this Part are the same, and differences that affect code are noted where they occur.

#### One service: order-service

The order service demonstrates database-per-service in code. It owns an `Order` aggregate, has a private datasource, and refers to customers and products only by identifier.

blocks.title: Order.java
OrderLine.java

blocks.text:
The price is copied into the order line at purchase time. This is a deliberate duplication: the order must record the price that was valid when it was placed, and a later change in the catalogue must not rewrite history. It also removes the need to join against the catalogue to display an old order.

The application service coordinates the use case. Its dependencies on other services are expressed as interfaces owned by the order service (`PriceLookup`, `StockReservation`), implemented in `infrastructure` with the HTTP clients introduced in the next chapter.

blocks.text: The comment on the last line marks a defect that the later chapters resolve: a remote call is made while a database transaction and its connection are held open, and the local commit and the remote reservation are not atomic. The corrected design replaces the inline call with a saga step and an outbox event.

blocks.text:
Reading the output: twenty serial dependencies of 99.9 percent each give about 98 percent, which corresponds to more than 14 hours of unavailability per month. The mitigation is not better individual services alone; it is fewer synchronous hops on the critical path, fallbacks that allow a request to succeed without a dependency, and asynchronous handling of everything that need not complete before the response.

blocks.text:
### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 1: the distributed monolith

**Scenario.** An organisation split a monolith into twelve services over a year. Releases are scheduled monthly because the services "must go out together".

**Symptoms.** A change to one field of the customer representation requires pull requests in five repositories merged in a fixed order. A staging environment with one service at an older version fails integration tests. An outage in the inventory service makes the catalogue pages return errors although they display no stock information.

**Diagnosis.** Three measurements locate the coupling. First, the deployment history: services whose release timestamps always fall within the same hour are coupled at deploy time. Second, the dependency graph taken from tracing data (a service map) or from the gateway access logs: a synchronous call from catalogue to inventory on a read path shows the failure propagation path. Third, schema ownership: `grep` for the other services' table names in each repository and inspect the database grants.

**Root cause.** Boundaries were drawn by technical layer or by entity rather than by business capability, services share a database or a shared DTO library, and calls are synchronous where the result is not needed to answer the request.

**Fix.** Replace the shared DTO library by per-consumer DTOs (consumer-driven contracts, see the chapter on API design). Replace synchronous calls on read paths by local read models fed by events. Merge services that always change together. Introduce an expand-and-contract policy for every interface change, so that old and new versions are accepted simultaneously.

**Prevention.** Track the lead time and the number of services touched per feature as architectural metrics. Require an independent deploy of each service in the pipeline (deploy the new version of a single service against the current versions of the others).

blocks.text:
#### Problem 2: schema change breaks another service

**Scenario.** The payment service reads the `orders` table of the order service directly "for reporting". A migration renames `total` to `total_amount`.

**Symptoms.** Payment captures begin to fail with `ERROR: column "total" does not exist` immediately after the order service is deployed; the order service itself is healthy and its tests pass.

**Diagnosis.** The PostgreSQL log names the failing statement and the role. Mapping the role to a service shows that the payment service holds a grant on the order service's schema. `SELECT grantee, privilege_type FROM` `information_schema.role_table_grants WHERE table_name = 'orders'` lists every consumer.

**Root cause.** The database is an integration point. Its schema became a public interface without versioning, review or tests.

**Fix.** Revoke the foreign grants. Expose the needed data through an API endpoint or an event, and have the payment service store the fields it needs (the order total at capture time) in its own table. For the transition, publish a database view with a stable name and version it like an API while consumers migrate.

**Prevention.** Provision one database role per service with privileges on its own schema only, and run the check query above in the pipeline.

#### Problem 3: a monolith decomposed too early

**Scenario.** A three-person team building a first product starts with eight services.

**Symptoms.** Most of the sprint is spent on build pipelines, version pinning and local environment start-up (eight processes, three databases and a broker); a feature that touches ordering and inventory needs two coordinated deployments; local integration testing needs the whole stack.

**Diagnosis.** Count the share of work items that touch more than one service, and compare the time spent on infrastructure tasks with feature tasks over a few sprints.

**Root cause.** The architecture was selected for an organisation size and scale that do not exist yet.

**Fix.** Merge the services into a modular monolith along the same boundaries (the package structure already exists), keep the module APIs as the former service interfaces, and extract a module only when a measured need appears (independent scaling, a separate team, a different availability target).

**Prevention.** Apply the decision path in the diagram: extraction requires a stated, measurable reason.

### Questions to expect

1. **What is the difference between a monolith, a modular monolith and microservices?** A monolith is one deployable unit with no enforced internal boundaries. A modular monolith is one deployable unit whose modules own their data and expose narrow APIs, enforced by tests or build rules. Microservices are separately deployable units with their own databases; the boundaries are network boundaries and consistency between them is eventual.
2. **What is a bounded context and why does it matter for service boundaries?** It is a boundary within which a domain model is consistent and each term has one meaning. Service boundaries aligned with bounded contexts minimise coupling because the same real-world entity is modelled separately in each context and shared only by identifier.
3. **Why database per service?** It makes the service the single owner of its schema, so schema changes do not require cross-team coordination, and it prevents hidden coupling through shared tables. The cost is the loss of cross-service joins and ACID transactions.
4. **What is a distributed monolith?** A system split into services that must still be deployed together and that fail together, typically because of a shared database, shared libraries with domain types, or chains of synchronous calls. It has the costs of both styles and the benefits of neither.
5. **How is the size of a service decided?** By data ownership and invariants, rate of change, team ownership and scaling profile, not by lines of code. Two entities that must be updated atomically belong in one service.
6. **When should microservices be avoided?** When the domain is unclear, the team is small, delivery automation and observability are missing, or strong cross-entity consistency is required.
7. **State Conway's law and a practical consequence.** System structure mirrors the communication structure of the organisation. The practical consequence is to organise teams around the desired service boundaries (inverse Conway manoeuvre) and give each service a single owning team.
8. **How is a monolith migrated to microservices safely?** With the strangler fig pattern: route traffic through a gateway, reimplement one capability at a time as a service, switch its route, and keep the old path available for rollback until the new service is verified.
9. **Why does availability decrease with more services?** Serial dependencies multiply availability: five services of 99.9 percent give about 99.5 percent. Mitigations are fewer synchronous hops, fallbacks, caching and asynchronous processing.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Microservices trade local simplicity for independent deployment; the trade is justified only by team scale, divergent scaling needs or isolation requirements.

- Boundaries follow bounded contexts and business capabilities, not technical layers or entity tables.
- Each service owns its data; cross-service joins and ACID transactions are replaced by composition, events and sagas.
- Availability multiplies and tail latency amplifies across synchronous hops, so the critical path is kept short.
- A modular monolith with enforced module boundaries is the default starting point; extraction needs a measurable reason.
- A distributed monolith (shared database, lockstep releases) is the characteristic failure of premature or poorly bounded decomposition.

A synchronous call blocks the caller, and the thread that issued it, until the callee answers or a timeout expires. It is the simplest interaction model and the one that most frequently causes production incidents, because every property of a local method call that a developer takes for granted is absent: the call can be slow, can fail after the work was performed, can be delivered twice, and can leave the caller waiting on a callee that has stopped responding. This chapter describes how an HTTP call is decomposed into separately bounded phases, how a timeout budget is derived across a chain of services, how retries are made safe with idempotency keys, and how the number of calls per request is controlled.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Protocol choices

REST over HTTP with JSON is the default for service-to-service calls that are also consumed by browsers and third parties. **gRPC** uses HTTP/2 with Protocol Buffers; the contract is a `.proto` file from which client stubs and server skeletons are generated, messages are binary and compact, calls are multiplexed over a long-lived connection, streaming is first class, and a call carries a deadline that is propagated automatically to downstream calls. Messaging (the Part on Kafka) is the alternative when the caller does not need an immediate answer.

blocks.text:
The remainder of the chapter uses HTTP and JSON, which the Spring Boot stack supports directly. The timeout, retry and idempotency principles apply unchanged to gRPC.

#### Client options in Spring Boot 3

Four client abstractions exist in a Boot 3 application, and the choice affects how timeouts and pools are configured.

- `RestClient` (Spring Framework 6.1, Boot 3.2 and later) is the synchronous fluent client and the recommended replacement for `RestTemplate` in new code. Boot provides a prototype `RestClient.Builder` bean pre-configured with message converters and an appropriate `ClientHttpRequestFactory`.
- `RestTemplate` is in maintenance mode. It remains supported and widely deployed; its behaviour with respect to timeouts and pools is identical because both delegate to a `ClientHttpRequestFactory`.
- `WebClient` is the reactive client. Using it from blocking code (calling `block()`) loses its benefits and is justified only when the rest of the stack is reactive.
- **HTTP interface clients** (`@HttpExchange` interfaces created with `HttpServiceProxyFactory`) describe a remote API as a Java interface; the proxy delegates to a `RestClient`, `WebClient` or `RestTemplate` through an adapter. Spring Cloud OpenFeign is documented as feature-complete and its documentation recommends migrating to HTTP interface clients. Spring Framework 7 (Boot 4) adds declarative registration of such clients; the Boot 3 idiom shown below creates the proxy explicitly.

Boot detects the HTTP library for `RestClient` and `RestTemplate` in this order: Apache HttpClient, Jetty HttpClient, Reactor Netty HttpClient, the JDK `java.net.http.HttpClient`, and finally `java.net.HttpURLConnection`. Since Boot 3.4 global defaults can be set with `spring.http.client.connect-timeout`, `spring.http.client.read-timeout`, `spring.http.client.redirects` and `spring.http.client.factory`; the reactive equivalents use the prefix `spring.http.reactiveclient`. A pool size or a per-phase timeout that these properties do not cover requires constructing the factory explicitly, as in the worked example.

#### The phases of one HTTP call

A call is a sequence of phases, and each phase has its own failure mode and its own timeout setting. Confusing them is the origin of most incidents attributed to "the network".

1. **Connection acquisition** from the client pool. If all connections to the route are in use, the caller waits in a queue. The bound is the pool acquisition timeout (Apache: `connectionRequestTimeout`).
2. **Connect**: TCP handshake, and the TLS handshake if used. The bound is the connect timeout. A failure here (refused, unreachable) means the request was never sent, so a retry is always safe.
3. **Send and wait for the first byte**: the callee processes the request. The bound is the read (socket) or response timeout. A failure here is ambiguous: the callee may have completed the work, partially completed it, or not started it.
4. **Receive the body.** A callee that sends headers and stalls is bounded by the same socket read timeout, applied per read, not to the whole response.

blocks.text:
No standard client timeout bounds the total duration of the exchange: a slow callee that sends one byte every second never triggers a read timeout of two seconds. An overall deadline is obtained with a time limiter (Resilience4j `TimeLimiter`, discussed in the resilience chapter), an HTTP/2 stream deadline, or a server-side budget.

#### Timeout budget across a chain

A request that crosses several services shares one budget. Each upstream timeout must exceed the total time its callee may spend, including retries, or the upstream gives up while the downstream continues to work on a result nobody will read. The relation for a caller that makes the downstream call with up to `n` attempts, a per-attempt timeout `t` and a delay `b` between attempts is:

**Budget rule**

blocks.code:
caller timeout  >  own work  +  n * t  +  (n - 1) * b  +  margin

example: gateway 3000 ms
  order-service   own work 100 ms, 2 attempts * 800 ms, 1 * 100 ms backoff  =  1800 ms
  margin          1200 ms          (3000 - 1800)

blocks.text:
The diagram also shows the cost that retries add on the callee: the abandoned first call is still executing. The callee should therefore be built to tolerate duplicated and abandoned work, which leads to idempotency.

#### Idempotency

An operation is **idempotent** if executing it several times has the same effect as executing it once. In HTTP, `GET`, `PUT`, `DELETE` and `HEAD` are defined as idempotent, and `POST` is not. A client may retry an idempotent request after an ambiguous failure without further protection. A `POST` that creates a payment or reserves stock must be made idempotent explicitly, and the standard technique is a client-generated **idempotency key**:

1. The client generates a unique key (a UUID) once per logical operation and sends it in a header (the convention `Idempotency-Key`), reusing the same value on every retry.
2. The server records the key together with a hash of the request and, when finished, the response, in a table with a unique constraint on the key.
3. A repeated request with a known key returns the stored response without repeating the work. A repeated key with a different request hash is a client error (HTTP 422).

The unique constraint is what makes the technique correct under concurrency: two simultaneous requests with the same key cannot both insert the row.

blocks.text:
#### Calls per request: the N+1 pattern across services

The N+1 selects problem has a distributed form. A list endpoint of the order service returns 50 orders and, for each, fetches the customer name from the customer service: one request for the list plus 50 requests for the customers. Every call adds serialisation, a network round trip and a slot in the callee's thread pool, and the latencies add up when the calls are sequential. Three remedies exist, in decreasing order of preference:

1. **Batch endpoint.** The callee offers `GET /customers?ids=...` (or a `POST` with a body when the list is long) and the caller makes one request for the distinct identifiers.
2. **Local read model.** The caller stores the few customer attributes it displays, updated from customer events. The call disappears from the read path entirely, at the price of eventual consistency.
3. **Bounded parallelism.** Independent calls are issued concurrently with virtual threads or a bounded executor. This reduces latency but not load, and unbounded parallelism turns the caller into a load generator against its dependency.

### Worked example

The order service needs prices from the catalog service and stock reservations from the inventory service. Both dependencies are described as HTTP interfaces; the inventory client carries an idempotency key.

The mapping of every 5xx answer to one exception type matters later: the retry and circuit-breaker configuration lists exactly the exception types that count as failures, and a 4xx answer (a client error) must not be counted, because retrying it cannot help and it does not indicate a sick dependency.

#### The callee: an idempotent payment endpoint

The payment service implements the server side of the idempotency key. In the simplest correct design the claim of the key and the business work run in one database transaction. A concurrent duplicate then blocks inside the database on the unique index until the first transaction finishes, and afterwards finds the committed row.

blocks.title: IdempotencyRecord.java
IdempotencyRepository.java
PaymentService.java

blocks.text: The `claim` statement is a native query because JPA has no portable equivalent of `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`; the alternative of saving an entity and catching `DataIntegrityViolationException` aborts the transaction in PostgreSQL, which makes the subsequent read fail with "current transaction is aborted". The row ends as part of the same commit as the payment, so a rollback of the business work also releases the key and the client may retry.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: The second design, claiming the key in its own short transaction with an `IN_PROGRESS` marker and completing it later, allows a concurrent duplicate to receive an immediate `409 Conflict` instead of waiting. It costs more code (a recovery job for keys stuck in `IN_PROGRESS` after a crash) and is justified when the business work is long. The SQL session below demonstrates this second design.

### Hands-on

The distributed N+1 effect is measurable with plain JDK classes. The program starts a small "customer service" that spends 5 ms per request, then fetches 50 customers three ways: sequentially, in parallel with virtual threads, and with one batch request.

The first version of this program, without the `sun.net.httpserver.nodelay` property, measured about 52 ms per request instead of about 9 ms. The server wrote the response headers and the body in two small segments, and the interaction of the Nagle algorithm with delayed acknowledgements on the client held the second segment for roughly 40 ms. The effect is a reminder that a measurement of a network call includes transport behaviour, and that a latency number of this kind has to be explained before it is accepted.

The idempotency table of the second design is exercised below in PostgreSQL 16, which was run for real. The `INSERT 0` `1` tag means one row was inserted (the key was claimed) and `INSERT 0 0` means the conflict clause suppressed the insert.

-- first request with key K1: claim the key
INSERT 0 1
-- retry arrives while the first is still running: claim fails (0 rows), caller must answer 409
INSERT 0 0
-- first request finishes: store the response
UPDATE 1
-- later retry: claim fails again, the stored response is replayed
INSERT 0 0

-----------+---------------+-----------------------------------------

(1 row)

blocks.text:
### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 1: the order list endpoint takes seconds (distributed N+1)

**Scenario.** `GET /api/v1/orders?size=50` of the order service enriches every order with the customer name by calling the customer service once per order.

**Symptoms.** The endpoint responds in 2 to 3 seconds in production and 80 ms in the developer environment. The customer service shows 50 times more requests than the order service on its dashboard, and its thread pool is busy although its CPU is idle.

**Diagnosis.** (1) The metric `http.client.requests` of the order service, filtered by the `uri` tag of the customer call, shows a request count 50 times the count of `http.server.requests` for the list endpoint. (2) A trace of one request shows 50 sequential child spans of identical name and duration below the controller span (see the chapter on tracing). (3) With debug logging of the client (`logging.level.org.springframework.web.client=DEBUG`) the log contains 50 lines `HTTP GET .../customers/{id}`.

**Root cause.** A loop over the result of the first query contains a remote call; locally the callee answers in about 1 ms, so the cost is invisible in development.

**Fix.** Add `GET /api/v1/customers?ids=` to the customer service, collect the distinct customer identifiers of the page, call once, and join in memory:

blocks.title: OrderQueryService.java (fragment)

blocks.text:
**Prevention.** Assert the number of outbound calls in an integration test with a stub server (for WireMock, `verify(1,` `getRequestedFor(urlPathEqualTo("/customers")))`), and set a maximum page size in the API.

#### Problem 2: customer charged twice after a timeout

**Scenario.** The order service calls `POST /payments`; the payment service captures the payment but is slow, the client times out and a retry interceptor repeats the request.

**Symptoms.** Customers report two charges for one order. The payment table contains two rows with the same `order_id` a few seconds apart.

**Diagnosis.** `SELECT order_id, count(*) FROM payment GROUP BY order_id HAVING count(*) > 1;` lists affected orders. The access log of the payment service contains two `POST /api/v1/payments` lines for the same order, the first with a duration above the client read timeout, which shows that the server completed work after the client had abandoned it.

**Root cause.** The retry policy treated `POST` like an idempotent method and the endpoint had no deduplication.

**Fix.** Introduce the `Idempotency-Key` header as in the worked example, and configure the retry to repeat only requests that carry a key or that use idempotent methods.

**Prevention.** A contract test per mutating endpoint that sends the same request twice with the same key and asserts a single side effect.

#### Problem 3: all endpoints hang when one dependency slows down (missing client timeout)

**Scenario.** The order service uses a `RestTemplate` created with `new RestTemplate()` for the inventory service. The inventory service begins to respond after 60 seconds or not at all.

**Symptoms.** After a few minutes every endpoint of the order service returns slowly or not at all, including `/actuator/health`, although the CPU is idle and the heap is small. Kubernetes liveness probes fail and the pods restart repeatedly.

**Diagnosis.** A thread dump shows the request threads waiting in the HTTP client. Taken with `jcmd <pid>` `Thread.print`, the dump contains many entries of this shape (typical output; frames differ by client library): **Thread dump excerpt (typical output, not run on the build machine)**

blocks.code:
"http-nio-8080-exec-37" #92 daemon prio=5
   java.lang.Thread.State: RUNNABLE
        at sun.nio.ch.NioSocketImpl.park(NioSocketImpl.java:186)
        at sun.nio.ch.NioSocketImpl.implRead(NioSocketImpl.java:312)
        at java.net.Socket$SocketInputStream.read(Socket.java:1099)
        at org.springframework.web.client.RestTemplate.execute(RestTemplate.java)
        at com.shop.order.infrastructure.InventoryGateway.reserve(InventoryGateway.java)

blocks.text:
Counting such threads (`jcmd <pid> Thread.print | grep -c "InventoryGateway.reserve"`) and comparing with the metric `tomcat.threads.busy` against `tomcat.threads.config.max` (the latter available when `server.tomcat.mbeanregistry.enabled=true`) confirms exhaustion of the 200 default worker threads.

**Root cause.** No read timeout was configured, so a stalled callee holds a worker thread indefinitely, and a few minutes of request arrivals consume the whole pool. The liveness probe is served by the same pool and fails as a consequence.

**Fix.** Set connect and read timeouts on every client (`spring.http.client.connect-timeout` and `spring.http.client.read-timeout` as defaults, or the explicit factory shown above), add a bulkhead so that one dependency cannot take all threads (see the resilience chapter), and serve liveness from a separate management port.

**Prevention.** A startup check or an architecture test that fails when a `RestClient` or `RestTemplate` is created without a configured factory, and a dashboard panel with busy threads against maximum threads.

### Questions to expect

1. **RestTemplate, RestClient or WebClient?** `RestClient` for new blocking code (Boot 3.2 and later); `RestTemplate` exists in large code bases and is in maintenance mode; `WebClient` when the application is reactive or needs streaming. All delegate to a pluggable HTTP library.
2. **Which timeouts does an HTTP client have?** Connection acquisition from the pool, connect, read (socket or response), and optionally a total deadline implemented outside the HTTP library. Each bounds a different phase and all should be set.
3. **Why is a retry unsafe after a read timeout?** The request may have been processed; the failure is ambiguous. Retrying a non-idempotent operation can duplicate its effect.
4. **How is a** `POST` **made safe to retry?** With an idempotency key generated by the client for each logical operation and stored by the server under a unique constraint together with the response.
5. **How are timeouts chosen across a chain?** Each upstream timeout must exceed the downstream's total time including retries; per-call timeouts are derived from the downstream p99 plus a margin, and the sum along the critical path stays below the user-facing timeout.
6. **What is the N+1 problem across services and how is it avoided?** One call per element of a list. Avoided with batch endpoints, local read models and bounded parallelism; detected by comparing client request counts with server request counts and by trace waterfalls.
7. **What does an HTTP interface client provide?** A Java interface with `@HttpExchange` annotations whose proxy performs the calls through a `RestClient`, `WebClient` or `RestTemplate`; it separates the description of a remote API from the transport configuration.
8. **When is gRPC preferable to REST?** For internal, high-volume calls with strict contracts and streaming needs, where generated stubs, binary payloads, multiplexing and built-in deadlines pay off; REST remains better for public and browser-facing APIs.
9. **Why map 5xx responses to a dedicated exception?** So that resilience configuration can state exactly which outcomes count as dependency failures; 4xx responses indicate a bad request and must not trip breakers or be retried.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Synchronous calls need explicit bounds, explicit repetition rules and an explicit budget.

- A call has four phases (acquire, connect, read, body); each needs its own timeout and none bounds the total, so a deadline must be added.
- Timeouts shrink along the chain: every upstream timeout exceeds the downstream total including retries.
- Retry only idempotent operations; make `POST` safe with an idempotency key stored under a unique constraint.
- Remote calls inside loops are the distributed N+1; use batch endpoints or local read models and verify the call count in tests.
- `RestClient` with an `@HttpExchange` interface is the Boot 3 idiom; map 5xx to a dedicated exception so resilience rules can name it.

Service instances are short-lived: a deployment replaces every instance, an autoscaler adds and removes instances, and a node failure relocates them. The address of an instance therefore cannot be written into the configuration of its callers. Three mechanisms remove that dependence. **Service discovery** maps a stable logical name to the current set of healthy instances. **Load balancing** selects one instance per request or per connection. **Externalised** **configuration** delivers environment-specific settings to every instance without rebuilding the artifact. A fourth component, the **API gateway**, provides the single entry point at which routing, authentication, rate limiting and edge resilience are applied once instead of in every service.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Discovery models

Two models exist. In **client-side discovery** each client obtains the list of instances from a registry (Eureka, Consul) and chooses among them itself; the registry is an additional component that every service registers with and that every caller queries. In **server-side discovery** the client addresses a stable name or virtual address and the platform picks the instance: a cloud load balancer, or on Kubernetes the `Service` object with its cluster DNS name (for example `inventory-service.shop.svc.cluster.local`, which resolves to a virtual IP that `kube-proxy` maps to the ready pods).

blocks.caption: Client-side registry (Eureka or Consul) compared with Kubernetes service discovery.

blocks.text:
On Kubernetes the registry adds no value and complicates operations: readiness already decides which pods receive traffic. The client-side model remains relevant on virtual machines and for features that need per-request control (zone preference, weighted routing, retry on a different instance). Spring Cloud Kubernetes provides a `DiscoveryClient` implementation backed by the Kubernetes API for the cases where a Spring client needs the instance list, but the default recommendation is to address the Service name directly.

#### How a registry works: Eureka as the reference

An Eureka client performs three periodic activities. It **registers** with the server at start-up. It sends a **heartbeat** (lease renewal) every 30 seconds by default. It **fetches the registry** delta and keeps a local cache that is refreshed on a timer; the lookups of the application use only this cache. The server removes an instance whose lease has not been renewed within the expiration duration (90 seconds by default, evicted by a periodic task). If too many leases lapse at once the server assumes a network partition and enters **self-preservation mode**, in which it stops evicting, preferring stale entries to a registry that empties during a partial outage.

blocks.text:
With the defaults mentioned (values to be confirmed for the version in use, since they are configurable and are not stated in the Spring Cloud reference), an instance killed without deregistering can still be selected for several minutes. The standard mitigations are graceful shutdown (the instance deregisters, then drains), retries that fall through to another instance on connection failure, and shortening the timers consciously, because the server's computations assume the heartbeat period.

#### Client-side load balancing with Spring Cloud LoadBalancer

Spring Cloud LoadBalancer is the client-side balancer of Spring Cloud. A client that uses a logical name (`http://inventory-service/...` or `lb://inventory-service` in a gateway route) is intercepted: `BlockingLoadBalancerClient` serves `RestClient` and `RestTemplate` beans marked `@LoadBalanced`, and a `ReactorLoadBalancerExchangeFilterFunction` serves `WebClient`. The interceptor asks a per-service `ReactorLoadBalancer` for an instance; the default implementation is `RoundRobinLoadBalancer`, with `RandomLoadBalancer` as the alternative. The candidate list comes from a `ServiceInstanceListSupplier`, which is composed from a delegate chain (discovery client, caching, health checks, zone preference, weighting, same-instance preference). Each logical service gets its own child application context, created lazily on first use unless `spring.cloud.loadbalancer.eager-load.clients` lists it.

Instance lists are cached; the documented defaults are a time to live of 35 seconds (`spring.cloud.loadbalancer.cache.ttl`) and a capacity of 256 entries. Load-balanced retry is controlled by `spring.cloud.loadbalancer.retry.enabled`. When a discovery client with its own cache (Eureka) is used, the second cache adds to the staleness window shown above.

The plain round-robin strategy ignores load: a slow instance receives the same share of requests as a fast one. Alternatives are weighted selection, a supplier that filters on health, and, at the platform level, least-connections balancing in the ingress or service mesh.

#### Kubernetes balances connections, not requests

`kube-proxy` makes a routing decision when a TCP connection is established. An HTTP client that keeps a connection alive and reuses it for thousands of requests sends all of them to the pod chosen at connect time. When a deployment scales from 2 to 6 pods, the existing connections stay on the original two pods and the new pods receive almost nothing; gRPC, which multiplexes all calls over one HTTP/2 connection, shows the effect most strongly. Remedies: a headless Service (`clusterIP: None`) with client-side balancing across the returned addresses, a maximum connection age on the client or server so that connections are recycled, an L7 proxy or service mesh that balances per request, or an ingress controller configured with a least-requests algorithm.

#### The API gateway

Spring Cloud Gateway is built on Spring WebFlux and Reactor Netty. Its building blocks are:

- **Route**: an identifier, a destination URI, a list of predicates and a list of filters.
- **Predicate**: a condition on the request (`Path`, `Method`, `Header`, `Host`, `Query`, `Cookie`, `After`, `Weight`). A route is selected when all its predicates match.
- **Filter**: logic applied before the request is forwarded (pre) and after the response returns (post): `StripPrefix`, `RewritePath`, `AddRequestHeader`, `Retry`, `CircuitBreaker`, `RequestRateLimiter`.
- **Global filter**: applied to every route (for example `ReactiveLoadBalancerClientFilter`, which resolves `lb://` URIs, and `NettyRoutingFilter`, which performs the forwarding).

Processing follows the WebFlux handler pipeline: `RoutePredicateHandlerMapping` evaluates the routes and stores the match in the exchange; `FilteringWebHandler` builds a `GatewayFilterChain` from the global filters and the route filters, sorted by `Ordered`; each filter may act before calling `chain.filter(exchange)` (pre phase) and in a continuation after it (post phase). The filter with the highest precedence (lowest order value) runs first on the way in and last on the way out.

blocks.text:
Version note: with the Spring Cloud 2025.0 release train (Gateway 4.3 and later, used with Boot 3.5) the artifact is named `spring-cloud-starter-gateway-server-webflux` and the properties live under `spring.cloud.gateway.server.webflux`; the earlier artifact `spring-cloud-starter-gateway` and the prefix `spring.cloud.gateway` apply to the 2024.0 train (Boot 3.4) and are deprecated afterwards. The examples below use the new names. A servlet-based variant (`spring-cloud-starter-gateway-server-webmvc`) exists for teams that prefer to stay on the blocking stack.

#### Rate limiting at the edge

`RequestRateLimiter` implements the **token bucket** algorithm: a bucket holds up to `burstCapacity` tokens, is refilled at `replenishRate` tokens per second, and each request removes `requestedTokens` (default 1); a request that finds the bucket empty receives HTTP 429. The state is kept in Redis (hence the dependency on `spring-boot-starter-data-redis-reactive`), which makes the limit global across all gateway instances. A `KeyResolver` bean decides what is limited: the authenticated user, an API key, or the client address. The mini gateway in the Hands-on section implements the same algorithm in memory.

#### Externalised configuration

Three mechanisms dominate in Spring applications.

1. **Environment variables and Kubernetes** `ConfigMap` **and** `Secret` **objects.** Values are injected as environment variables (read once at pod start) or mounted as files. Boot can import a mounted directory with `spring.config.import=optional:configtree:/etc/config/`, where each file name becomes a property key and its content the value; this is the usual way to consume mounted Secrets.
2. **Spring Cloud Config Server**, a service that serves property files from a Git repository (or another backend) per application name and profile. Clients declare `spring.config.import=optional:configserver:http://config-server:8888`. A change in Git becomes visible after the client refreshes (`POST /actuator/refresh` re-binds `@ConfigurationProperties` and rebuilds `@RefreshScope` beans).
3. **Cloud-provider or Vault stores**, imported through further `spring.config.import` locations.

Precedence, from highest to lowest, follows the order documented for Boot: command-line arguments, system properties, environment variables, imported and profile-specific files, then defaults packaged in the JAR. A value that is set in two places is a latent source of drift.

        webflux:
          httpclient:
            connect-timeout: 500          # milliseconds
            response-timeout: 3s          # java.time.Duration
          routes:
            - id: orders
              uri: http://order-service:8080
              predicates:
                - Path=/api/orders/**
              filters:
                - RewritePath=/api/orders(?<segment>/?.*), /api/v1/orders${segment}
                - name: RequestRateLimiter
                  args:
                    redis-rate-limiter.replenishRate: 20
                    redis-rate-limiter.burstCapacity: 40
                    redis-rate-limiter.requestedTokens: 1
                    key-resolver: "#{@clientKeyResolver}"
                - name: Retry
                  args:
                    retries: 2
                    methods: GET
                    statuses: BAD_GATEWAY, SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE
                    backoff:
                      firstBackoff: 50ms
                      maxBackoff: 500ms
                      factor: 2
                      basedOnPreviousValue: false
                - name: CircuitBreaker
                  args:
                    name: ordersBreaker
                    fallbackUri: forward:/fallback/orders
            - id: reports
              uri: http://report-service:8080
              predicates:
                - Path=/api/reports/**
              metadata:
                response-timeout: 20000     # per-route override in milliseconds
                connect-timeout: 500

management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info,prometheus,gateway

blocks.text: The `Retry` filter is limited to `GET` and to two gateway-class statuses; a `POST` is never retried by the gateway because the gateway cannot know whether the operation is idempotent. The `gateway` actuator endpoint (`/actuator/gateway/routes`) lists the effective routes and is the first diagnostic tool when a route does not match. On the 2024.0 release train the same file is written with `spring.cloud.gateway.routes` and `spring.cloud.gateway.httpclient`, without the `server.webflux` levels.

blocks.text: The Kubernetes side of the same system consists of a `Service`, which provides the stable name, and a `ConfigMap`, which provides the non-secret configuration. The checksum annotation forces a rolling restart when the ConfigMap changes, which closes the drift problem described below.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: order-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: order-service
  ports:
    - port: 8080
      targetPort: 8080
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: order-service-config
data:
  clients.inventory.base-url: "http://inventory-service:8080"
  resilience.timeout: "800ms"
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: order-service
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: order-service
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: order-service
      annotations:
        checksum/config: "<sha256 of the ConfigMap, computed by Helm or the pipeline>"
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: order-service
          image: registry.example.com/shop/order-service:1.4.2
          env:
            - name: SPRING_CONFIG_IMPORT
              value: "optional:configtree:/etc/config/"
          volumeMounts:
            - name: config

        - name: config

### Hands-on

The behaviour of the gateway pipeline, round-robin selection, failover on a failed instance, path rewriting and token-bucket limiting is reproduced with plain JDK classes (`com.sun.net.httpserver` and `java.net.http`). The program starts four backend instances and a gateway, then sends requests.

Run the mini gateway (request ids and the number of admitted requests vary with timing)

blocks.text:
Observations. The first six requests rotate over `order-1`, `order-2`, `order-3`. The prefix `/api` is stripped before forwarding, which is the effect of `StripPrefix=1`. After `order-2` is stopped, the first request routed to it fails with a connection error, the gateway marks the instance down for two seconds (a passive health check) and retries the same request on the next instance, so the client sees no error; the request ids skip a number because the failed attempt consumed one. Six rather than five of the eight rapid requests passed the limiter because the bucket refills at five tokens per second while the requests are being issued.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 1: gateway returns 504 although the service completed the work

**Scenario.** The gateway has `response-timeout: 3s`. The order service takes 3.4 seconds for a checkout during a database slowdown.

**Symptoms.** Clients receive `504 Gateway Timeout` and retry. The order table later contains two orders for one cart. The order service logs show the request completing successfully after the client was gone.

**Diagnosis.** Compare timestamps: the gateway access log shows the 504 at 3.0 s, the order service shows the completion at 3.4 s. The metric `spring.cloud.gateway.requests` (tags `routeId`, `status`) shows the 504 count rising on the route. `GET /actuator/gateway/routes` shows the effective route configuration, including any per-route `response-timeout` metadata.

**Root cause.** The timeouts do not form a budget: the service has no deadline shorter than the gateway's, so it continues to work for a client that has already been answered, and the client's retry creates a duplicate.

**Fix.** Order the timeouts: client greater than gateway greater than service call chain. Give the service its own bounded work (query timeout via `spring.jpa.properties.jakarta.persistence.query.timeout`, client timeouts as in the previous chapter), set long-running routes explicitly through the `response-timeout` metadata, and make checkout idempotent.

**Prevention.** Keep the budget table (client, gateway, service, database timeouts) in the repository next to the configuration and review it with every timeout change.

#### Problem 2: 503 and connection errors for minutes after each deployment

**Scenario.** A rolling update replaces the pods of the inventory service. During each deployment the order service logs `Connection refused` and `503` for a few minutes.

**Symptoms.** The error rate spikes at every release and recovers without intervention. Pods that were terminated are still receiving requests.

**Diagnosis.** (1) `kubectl get endpoints inventory-service -w` while the rollout runs shows when the old addresses disappear. (2) Compare the timestamp of the pod termination with the last request logged by that pod. (3) For a registry-based setup, `GET /eureka/apps/INVENTORY-SERVICE` shows entries for instances that no longer exist, and the metric or log of the load balancer cache shows the 35 second window.

**Root cause.** Termination and endpoint removal are asynchronous. On Kubernetes, the pod receives SIGTERM at about the same moment that the endpoint is removed from the Service; components that have not yet observed the change keep sending requests. In a registry model the staleness window is the sum of the timers in the earlier diagram.

**Fix.** Enable graceful shutdown (`server.shutdown=graceful` with `spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase=30s`), add a `preStop` hook with a short sleep (for example five seconds) so that the endpoint removal propagates before the server stops accepting connections, make readiness fail first, and let clients retry idempotent calls on a different instance.

**Prevention.** A deployment test that runs a constant request load during a rolling update and fails the pipeline on any non-2xx result.

blocks.text:
#### Problem 3: one instance behaves differently (configuration drift)

**Scenario.** Rate limiting is configured as 20 requests per second in the ConfigMap. One of five gateway pods rejects clients at 10 requests per second.

**Symptoms.** Intermittent 429 responses for the same client; identical requests behave differently depending on the pod that serves them.

**Diagnosis.** Compare the effective configuration of each pod: `kubectl exec <pod> -- env | grep -i rate`, `GET` `/actuator/env/<property>` (the response lists every property source that defines the value and which one won) and `GET /actuator/configprops` for bound beans (both endpoints require exposure and protection; see the Actuator chapter). A pod that started before the ConfigMap edit has the old value because environment variables are read once at start-up.

**Root cause.** The ConfigMap was edited in place. Pods that consume it as environment variables keep the old values until restarted, and pods that mount it as a volume receive the new file after the kubelet sync delay, but Boot reads the files only at start-up unless a refresh is triggered.

**Fix.** Treat configuration as part of the release: add the checksum annotation shown above so that a ConfigMap change causes a rolling restart, or use Spring Cloud Config or Kubernetes configuration reload with an explicit refresh.

**Prevention.** Expose the effective value of critical settings as a metric or an info contribution, and alert when instances of one application report different values.

#### Problem 4: new pods receive no traffic after scaling out

**Scenario.** The inventory service is scaled from 2 to 6 pods during a sale; latency on the original two pods does not improve.

**Symptoms.** CPU of two pods at saturation, four pods idle; the request rate per pod is uneven.

**Diagnosis.** Per-pod request rate (`http.server.requests` grouped by pod label); the number of established connections per pod (`ss -tn state established | grep :8080 | wc -l` inside each pod); client pool settings show a small pool of long-lived keep-alive connections.

**Root cause.** The clients hold persistent connections created before the scale-out, and `kube-proxy` balanced those connections, not the requests.

**Fix.** Limit connection lifetime on the clients (the Apache `ConnectionConfig` time-to-live, for example 30 seconds) or on the server (`server.tomcat.keep-alive-timeout` and `server.tomcat.max-keep-alive-requests`), or use a request-level balancer.

**Prevention.** Scale-out is validated in load tests by checking the per-pod request distribution, not only the aggregate latency.

### Questions to expect

1. **Why is service discovery needed?** Instances are ephemeral and their addresses change; callers need a stable logical name that resolves to the currently healthy instances.
2. **Client-side versus server-side discovery?** Client-side: the client queries a registry and balances itself (Eureka plus Spring Cloud LoadBalancer), giving per-request control at the cost of library coupling. Server-side: the platform balances (Kubernetes Service), keeping clients simple but balancing per connection.
3. **Do Spring applications on Kubernetes need Eureka?** Normally not; the Service DNS name and readiness probes provide discovery and health filtering. Eureka remains useful off Kubernetes.

#### 4. What is the default load-balancing algorithm of Spring Cloud LoadBalancer? Round robin

(`RoundRobinLoadBalancer`); a random implementation is available, and the instance list comes from a `ServiceInstanceListSupplier` chain.

1. **What does an API gateway do and what should it not do?** It routes, authenticates, rate limits, applies edge resilience and adds correlation data. It should not contain business logic, because it is shared by all teams and becomes a deployment bottleneck.
2. **How does the gateway filter chain work?** The matched route and the global filters form an ordered chain; each filter has a pre phase before calling the chain and a post phase afterwards; the highest precedence runs first on the way in and last on the way out.
3. **How does** `RequestRateLimiter` **work and where is the state?** Token bucket with `replenishRate` and `burstCapacity`, state in Redis so that the limit holds across gateway instances; a `KeyResolver` selects the limited identity; excess requests receive 429.
4. **How is configuration kept consistent across instances?** One source of truth (ConfigMap or Config Server), rolled out through the release process, with a restart or an explicit refresh and with the effective values observable at run time.
5. **Why can scaling out not help immediately on Kubernetes?** The Service balances connections; long-lived keep-alive or HTTP/2 connections remain pinned to the old pods.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Discovery, balancing, gateway and configuration decide how a request finds a healthy, correctly configured instance.

- On Kubernetes the Service name is the discovery mechanism and `kube-proxy` balances connections; client-side registries remain for non-Kubernetes platforms.
- Spring Cloud Gateway evaluates predicates, then runs an ordered chain of global and route filters with pre and post phases; rate limiting is a Redis-backed token bucket.
- Registry staleness is the sum of lease, eviction and cache timers; graceful shutdown, preStop delay and retries cover the gap.
- Timeouts form a budget (client, gateway, service); a gateway timeout without a bounded service produces duplicate work.
- Configuration drift is prevented by treating configuration as a release artifact: checksum-triggered rollouts and observable effective values.

sections.title: Resilience: Timeouts, Retries, Circuit Breakers and Bulkheads

blocks.text:
### Bulkheads

A dependency that fails quickly is an inconvenience; a dependency that responds slowly is an outage. A failed call releases its thread within milliseconds, whereas a slow call holds a thread, a pooled connection and often a database transaction for as long as the call lasts, and the caller's capacity is consumed by requests that cannot complete. Resilience engineering for services is therefore concerned with bounding the damage that one slow or failing component can cause to the components that depend on it. The mechanisms in this chapter are timeouts, retries with backoff and jitter, circuit breakers, bulkheads, rate limiters, fallbacks and load shedding. Each addresses a specific failure mode, and several of them cause incidents of their own when combined carelessly; the chapter pays as much attention to those interactions as to the mechanisms.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Why slowness cascades

Little's law relates the average number of requests in a system (`L`) to the arrival rate (`λ`) and the average time each spends in it (`W`): `L = λ × W`. A service that receives 100 requests per second and answers in 20 ms holds two requests in flight on average. If one of its dependencies begins to answer in 5 seconds, the same arrival rate requires `100 × 5 =` `500` concurrent requests. A Tomcat pool of 200 threads is exhausted within about two seconds; from then on new requests queue, wait for the accept queue, and time out in the caller, which in turn begins to accumulate waiting threads. The failure moves up the call chain at the speed of the thread pools filling.

blocks.text:
The defences operate at different points of this process. A **timeout** limits how long one call may hold a thread. A **bulkhead** limits how many threads one dependency may hold. A **circuit breaker** stops sending calls to a dependency that is known to be failing, so that no thread is spent on it at all. **Load shedding** refuses work early when the service itself is saturated. A **fallback** supplies a degraded answer instead of an error.

#### Timeouts

Timeouts are the foundation, since every other mechanism relies on calls that end. The phases and the budget rule were described in the chapter on synchronous communication. Resilience4j adds the `TimeLimiter`, which bounds the total duration of an asynchronous call (`CompletableFuture` or other `CompletionStage`) and can cancel it; its configuration keys are `timeoutDuration` and `cancelRunningFuture`. A `TimeLimiter` cannot interrupt a blocking method that is called synchronously from the caller's thread, so for blocking `RestClient` code the client library timeouts remain the effective bound.

#### Retries, backoff and jitter

A retry converts a transient failure (a dropped connection, a pod being replaced, a short overload) into a success at the cost of extra load and extra latency. Three conditions must hold for a retry to be correct: the failure is plausibly transient, the operation is idempotent or protected by a key, and the extra load does not endanger the dependency.

**Backoff** spaces the attempts: the delay before attempt `n` grows exponentially, `delay(n) = base × multiplier^(n-1)`, optionally capped. **Jitter** randomises the delay. Without jitter, clients that failed at the same instant (because the same dependency failed) retry at the same instants, so the dependency receives synchronised waves just as it tries to recover. Two common schemes are full jitter (a uniform random delay between zero and the exponential value) and equal jitter (half of the exponential value plus a random half). Resilience4j exposes this as `enableExponentialBackoff`, `exponentialBackoffMultiplier`, `enableRandomizedWait` and `randomizedWaitFactor`.

blocks.text: The more serious hazard is **retry amplification**. If each of three layers in a call chain (gateway, order service, inventory client) retries three times, one user request produces `3 × 3 × 3 = 27` calls against the failing dependency. A dependency that was overloaded at 100 requests per second now receives 2700 per second: the retries convert a partial failure into a total one, which is a **retry storm**. The rules that prevent it are retry at one layer only (usually the one closest to the failing call), a small attempt count, a retry budget (for example, allow retries only up to 10 percent of the request volume), and no retry when the circuit is open.

blocks.text:
#### Circuit breaker

A circuit breaker wraps a call and observes its outcomes. While the dependency is healthy it is transparent. When the observed failure rate exceeds a threshold it opens and rejects calls immediately without touching the dependency, which protects the caller's threads and gives the dependency room to recover. After a wait period it lets a limited number of probe calls through; their result decides whether to close or to open again.

failure rate \>= 50% or slow-call rate \>= 80% **CLOSED OPEN** **calls pass; outcomes recorded calls rejected at once** *(after minimumNumberOfCalls)* **in a sliding window CallNotPermittedException**

probes succeed probes fail (failure rate \< 50%)

**HALF\_OPEN** wait duration elapsed (10 s) **n probe calls admitted** **others rejected**

*Figure 4.18. The three states and the conditions of each transition; the open state rejects calls with* `CallNotPermittedException`*,* *and the half-open state admits only a limited number of probes.*

The parameters of the Resilience4j breaker, with the documented defaults:

rows: the window is the last N calls, or the last N seconds (TIME\_BASED)
window size in calls or seconds
calls needed before the failure rate is evaluated at all
percentage of failures that opens the breaker
a call longer than this counts as slow
percentage of slow calls that opens the breaker
move to HALF\_OPEN by timer, not on the next call
which exceptions count as failures, and which are neutral
blocks.caption: Resilience4j circuit breaker configuration properties.

blocks.text:
Two defaults deserve attention. `minimumNumberOfCalls` equal to 100 means that a service with ten calls per minute needs more than ten minutes of traffic before the breaker can open at all. `waitDurationInOpenState` of 60 seconds keeps a recovered dependency isolated for a minute after it has returned. Both are rarely appropriate unchanged. The slow-call settings are valuable because most real outages present first as latency, not as errors.

What counts as a failure is a design decision: timeouts, connection errors and 5xx responses indicate a sick dependency and are recorded; 4xx responses and business rejections (insufficient stock) are the dependency working correctly and must be ignored, or a burst of invalid requests would open the breaker.

#### Bulkhead

A bulkhead partitions capacity, as the compartments of a ship limit the spread of flooding. The **semaphore bulkhead** limits the number of concurrent calls to a dependency (`maxConcurrentCalls`, default 25) and rejects excess calls after `maxWaitDuration` (default 0, which means immediately) with `BulkheadFullException`. The **thread-pool bulkhead** executes the calls on a dedicated pool with a queue, isolating them completely from the caller's threads; it requires asynchronous invocation and costs a thread hand-off. The semaphore variant is sufficient for most blocking Spring applications.

blocks.text:
#### Rate limiter, load shedding and fallbacks

A **client-side rate limiter** (`limitForPeriod`, `limitRefreshPeriod`, `timeoutDuration`) protects a dependency with a known quota (a payment provider with 50 requests per second). A **server-side limiter** at the gateway protects the system from abusive or runaway clients. **Load shedding** is the server protecting itself: when a queue exceeds a bound the service answers `503 Service Unavailable` with a `Retry-After` header at once instead of accepting work it cannot finish. In Spring Boot the relevant Tomcat settings are `server.tomcat.threads.max`, `server.tomcat.accept-count` (the queue of pending connections) and `server.tomcat.max-connections`; an application-level limiter such as a semaphore around expensive endpoints gives finer control.

A **fallback** is an alternative result when the primary call fails or is rejected. Useful forms are a cached or last-known value (a stale price is better than no price), a default (an empty recommendation list), a simplified computation, and a queued request processed later. A fallback that hides a failure which the caller must act on is harmful: for a stock reservation the correct reaction to a failed call is to reject the order, not to assume success. The design question for each dependency is whether degraded operation is acceptable, and if so, in what form; this is **graceful degradation**.

#### Composition order

Resilience4j annotations and decorators are proxy-based, and the order in which they wrap the call matters. The default aspect order is Retry outermost, then CircuitBreaker, RateLimiter, TimeLimiter, Bulkhead innermost, which is written `Retry(CircuitBreaker(RateLimiter(TimeLimiter(Bulkhead(call)))))`. The order is adjustable through `resilience4j.retry.retryAspectOrder`, `circuitBreakerAspectOrder` and the equivalent keys (a higher value means higher priority).

blocks.text: The fallback method has the same parameters as the protected method plus a trailing exception parameter and the same return type; Resilience4j selects the most specific matching fallback. The fallback is attached to `@Retry`, the outermost decorator, deliberately: a fallback on the inner `@CircuitBreaker` would convert every failure into `StockUnavailableException` before the retry could see it, and since that type is not listed in `retryExceptions` no retry would ever occur. On the outermost decorator it runs only after the retries are exhausted, and it also receives `CallNotPermittedException` and `BulkheadFullException`. The fallback rethrows a domain exception because a reservation cannot be assumed: the order service answers the caller with `503` and a `Retry-After` header (see the chapter on API design), and the order is not created.

blocks.code:
resilience4j:
  circuitbreaker:
    configs:
      default:
        slidingWindowType: COUNT_BASED
        slidingWindowSize: 20
        minimumNumberOfCalls: 10
        failureRateThreshold: 50
        slowCallDurationThreshold: 1s
        slowCallRateThreshold: 80
        waitDurationInOpenState: 10s
        permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState: 5
        automaticTransitionFromOpenToHalfOpenEnabled: true
        registerHealthIndicator: true
        recordExceptions:
          - com.shop.order.infrastructure.DependencyUnavailableException
          - org.springframework.web.client.ResourceAccessException
        ignoreExceptions:
          - org.springframework.web.client.HttpClientErrorException
    instances:
      inventory:
        baseConfig: default
  retry:
    instances:
      inventory:
        maxAttempts: 3
        waitDuration: 100ms
        enableExponentialBackoff: true
        exponentialBackoffMultiplier: 2
        enableRandomizedWait: true
        randomizedWaitFactor: 0.5
        retryExceptions:
          - com.shop.order.infrastructure.DependencyUnavailableException
          - org.springframework.web.client.ResourceAccessException
        ignoreExceptions:
          - io.github.resilience4j.circuitbreaker.CallNotPermittedException
  bulkhead:
    instances:
      inventory:
        maxConcurrentCalls: 20
        maxWaitDuration: 0

management:
  health:
    circuitbreakers:
    enabled: true
endpoints:
  web:
    exposure:
      include: health,prometheus,circuitbreakers,circuitbreakerevents,retries,bulkheads
blocks.title: order-service/src/main/resources/application.yml (resilience part)

blocks.text:
Points that the configuration encodes. Retry and breaker list the same two exception types as failures, which excludes 4xx responses. The retry ignores `CallNotPermittedException`, so an open breaker ends the call immediately instead of consuming the retry attempts. The slow-call threshold (1 second) is above the HTTP client's 800 ms read timeout, so timeouts count as failures and the slow-call rule catches a dependency that answers just inside the timeout. The bulkhead limit (20) is below the Tomcat pool size (200), so the inventory service can never take more than a tenth of the worker threads.

State transitions are logged through the event publisher; the listener documents the breaker's decisions in the log, which is the first evidence examined during an incident:

blocks.text:
Reading the result. Without the breaker the caller was blocked for 2.6 seconds in total and every call during the outage waited for its full timeout. With the breaker the dependency received 44 instead of 70 calls, the caller blocked for 1.3 seconds, and 26 calls were answered in microseconds with a rejection that the application can turn into a fallback. The five timeouts before the opening are the price of detection; the window and the minimum call count control that price. The breaker did not return to CLOSED at the end of the outage (t=2000) but at 2172 ms, because the open period of one second began at 1014 ms and lasted until 2050 ms.

The third program shows the effect of a bulkhead on an endpoint that does not use the failing dependency.
